Count moles of ATOMS in each sample.

(A) 2 mol cyclohexane \(C_{6}H_{12}\): each molecule has \(6 + 12 = 18\) atoms, so \(2 \times 18 = 36\) mol of atoms.

(B) Sucrose \(C_{12}H_{22}O_{11}\), \(M = 12(12) + 22(1) + 11(16) = 342\ g\ mol^{-1}\). Moles \(= 684/342 = 2\). Each molecule has \(12 + 22 + 11 = 45\) atoms, so \(2 \times 45 = 90\) mol of atoms.

(C) At STP \(1\) mol of gas occupies \(22.7\ L\), so \(90.8/22.7 = 4\) mol \(H_{2}\). Being diatomic this is \(4 \times 2 = 8\) mol of atoms. (Even with the older \(22.4\ L\) value the result is only \(8.1\) mol of atoms.)

Therefore \(90 > 36 > 8\), i.e. \((B) > (A) > (C)\).

With the internuclear axis along \(z\), the \(\pi\) molecular orbitals are built from the \(p_{x}\) (or \(p_{y}\)) orbitals, which lie perpendicular to that axis. The ANTIBONDING combination \(\pi^{*}\) is the out-of-phase overlap, so it must show TWO nodal features: (i) the nodal plane containing the internuclear axis that every \(\pi\) orbital has, and (ii) an additional nodal plane between the two nuclei arising from the sign reversal.

Reading the four pictures: one shows a single lobe above and a single lobe below the axis spanning both nuclei (that is the bonding \(\pi\)); one shows four lobes lying head-on ALONG the axis (that is \(\sigma^{*}\) from \(p_{z}\)); one shows the two side-on lobes with the SAME shading top and bottom on both atoms (in-phase, again bonding \(\pi\)). Only option (C) shows the two side-on \(p\) orbitals with opposite phases, shaded lobe up on the left atom and shaded lobe down on the right atom, giving the required node between the nuclei. Hence (C) is the \(\pi^{*}\) orbital.

Osmotic pressure is colligative, so compare the total particle concentrations across the membrane AB.

Side x: \(0.1\ M\ K_{4}[Fe(CN)_{6}] \rightarrow 4K^{+} + [Fe(CN)_{6}]^{4-}\), so \(i = 5\) and the effective particle concentration is \(0.1 \times 5 = 0.5\ M\).
Side y: \(0.1\ M\ FeCl_{3} \rightarrow Fe^{3+} + 3Cl^{-}\), so \(i = 4\) and the effective concentration is \(0.1 \times 4 = 0.4\ M\).

Side x is therefore the more concentrated (hypertonic) solution and side y is hypotonic, making (C) correct.

The others fail: (A) no Prussian-blue colour can form because a semipermeable membrane passes only solvent, so the two solutes never meet; (B) is the direct denial of that same fact; (D) is wrong because solvent flows spontaneously from y to x, and to reverse it the applied pressure on x must EXCEED the osmotic pressure difference, not merely be 'any value'.

(A) Williamson synthesis: an alkoxide \(RO^{-}\) attacks a primary alkyl halide and displaces the halide, so it is NUCLEOPHILIC SUBSTITUTION, an \(S_{N}2\) process - matches (III).

(B) Friedel-Crafts reaction: \(AlCl_{3}\) generates \(R^{+}\) or \(RCO^{+}\), which attacks the aromatic ring, so it is ELECTROPHILIC SUBSTITUTION - matches (IV).

(C) Bromination of vinyl benzene (styrene): \(Br_{2}\) adds across the \(C=C\) side chain through a bromonium ion, so it is ELECTROPHILIC ADDITION - matches (I).

(D) Chlorination of toluene in light: light homolyses \(Cl_{2}\) and the benzylic \(C-H\) is substituted through a benzyl radical, so it is FREE RADICAL SUBSTITUTION - matches (II).

Hence (A)-(III), (B)-(IV), (C)-(I), (D)-(II).

Ionization is always an ENDOTHERMIC process, so every ionization enthalpy is positive; this immediately rules out the two negative options \(-906\) and \(-856\ kJ/mol\).

Removing a second electron is from a species that is already positively charged, so the electron is held more tightly and \(IE_{2} > IE_{1}\) always. This rules out \(+590\ kJ/mol\), which is smaller than the given \(IE_{1} = +737\ kJ/mol\).

Only \(+1450\ kJ/mol\) is both positive and larger than \(737\ kJ/mol\); it is also the accepted value for the second ionization enthalpy of Mg (still a modest jump because the second electron also comes from the \(3s\) orbital, the very large jump appearing only at \(IE_{3}\), where the neon core is broken).

Ge has a Pauling electronegativity of \(2.01\), i.e. \(2.0\) to one decimal place. In group 13 the element matching this is thallium (\(2.04 \rightarrow 2.0\)), and the statements below only make sense for Tl.

Because of the inert pair effect, which is strongest at the bottom of group 13, \(Tl^{+}\) is far more stable than \(Tl^{3+}\). Consequently:
(A) FALSE - \(Tl^{3+}\) does not lose more electrons, so it is not a reducing agent.
(B) TRUE - \(Tl^{3+}\) readily accepts two electrons to fall back to the stable \(Tl^{+}\), so it is a strong oxidising agent.
(C) FALSE - the reverse holds; \(E^{+}\) is the more stable ion.
(D) TRUE - \(E^{\circ}(Tl^{3+}/Tl) = +0.72\ V\), a positive value, consistent with the reluctance of Tl to exist in the \(+3\) state.

So (B) and (D) only.

In all three complexes nickel is \(Ni^{2+}\), a \(d^{8}\) ion.

Unpaired electrons: for an octahedral \(d^{8}\) ion the configuration is \(t_{2g}^{6}e_{g}^{2}\) whatever the field strength, because the two \(e_{g}\) electrons must occupy the two separate \(e_{g}\) orbitals - so both \([Ni(en)_{3}]^{2+}\) and \([Ni(NH_{3})_{6}]^{2+}\) have 2 unpaired electrons. For tetrahedral \([NiCl_{4}]^{2-}\) the configuration is \(e^{4}t_{2}^{3}\)... more precisely \(e^{4}t_{2}^{4}\), which again leaves 2 unpaired electrons. So the count is 2, 2, 2.

Frequency of absorption is proportional to the splitting energy \(\Delta\). Ligand field strength runs \(en > NH_{3} > Cl^{-}\), and in addition \(\Delta_{t} \approx \frac{4}{9}\Delta_{o}\), so a tetrahedral chloro complex has by far the smallest splitting. Hence \(\Delta\) and therefore the absorption frequency follow \((A) > (C) > (B)\).

The matching option is '2, 2, 2 and \((A) > (C) > (B)\)'.

The three species read from the figures are (x) tropone, the seven-membered cyclohepta-2,4,6-trien-1-one; (y) a simple ketone, \(CH_{3}COCH_{3}\); and (z) the acetate ion \(CH_{3}COO^{-}\).

Bond length rises as bond ORDER falls, so rank by how much single-bond character resonance introduces into the carbon-oxygen bond.

(y) A plain ketone has an essentially pure \(C=O\) double bond (bond order 2), so its bond is the SHORTEST.

(z) In acetate the negative charge is delocalised over two equivalent oxygens; the two contributing structures are degenerate, so each carbon-oxygen bond has bond order exactly \(1.5\) and is longer than a ketone \(C=O\).

(x) In tropone the dipolar structure places a negative charge on oxygen and a positive charge on the ring, which then becomes the six-electron aromatic tropylium cation. That aromatic stabilisation makes the dipolar form an unusually heavy contributor (tropone has an exceptionally large dipole moment, about \(4.3\ D\) against \(2.9\ D\) for acetone), so the carbon-oxygen bond acquires the greatest single-bond character and is the LONGEST.

Hence \((x) > (z) > (y)\).

The highest manganese oxide is \(Mn_{2}O_{7}\) (Mn in \(+7\)); oxygen stabilises higher oxidation states through multiple bonding. Hence \(|x| = |4 - 7| = 3\).

Read the plot of \([R]\) against \(t\). Curve 1 falls as a STRAIGHT LINE, and a linear concentration-time plot is the signature of a ZERO order reaction. Curves 2 and 3 are exponential-looking decays, characteristic of first (or higher) order.

(a) FALSE - curve 1 is zero order while curves 2 and 3 are not, so the three orders are not the same.
(b) TRUE - for a common order, the reaction whose concentration falls faster has the larger rate constant. Curve 3 drops away more steeply than curve 2 from the same \([R]_{0}\), so \(k_{3} > k_{2}\).
(c) FALSE - reaction 1 is zero order, whose rate law is \(rate = k\), giving \(k\) the units \(mol\ L^{-1}\ s^{-1}\), not \(s^{-1}\).
(d) FALSE - thermal decomposition of HI on a gold surface is the standard example of a ZERO order reaction, so it corresponds to curve 1, not curve 2.

Only the second statement is correct.

Compound (X) in the scheme is styrene, \(C_{6}H_{5}CH=CH_{2}\).

(i) \(Br_{2}/CHCl_{3}\) adds across the double bond to give the vicinal dibromide \(C_{6}H_{5}CHBr-CH_{2}Br\).

(ii) Excess \(NaNH_{2}\) eliminates HBr twice (double dehydrohalogenation) to give phenylacetylene \(C_{6}H_{5}C \equiv CH\); the excess base then removes the acidic terminal alkyne proton to give the sodium acetylide \(C_{6}H_{5}C \equiv C^{-}Na^{+}\).

(iii) \(CH_{3}I\) alkylates the acetylide by \(S_{N}2\), giving 1-phenylpropyne \(C_{6}H_{5}C \equiv C-CH_{3}\).

(iv) \(Na/NH_{3}(l)\) is a dissolving-metal reduction, which reduces the internal alkyne stereoselectively to the TRANS alkene, \((E)\)-1-phenylpropene \(C_{6}H_{5}CH=CH-CH_{3}\).

Product (Y) is \(C_{9}H_{10}\), so \(M = 9(12) + 10(1) = 108 + 10 = 118\ g\ mol^{-1}\).

Look at the four groups on the central carbon in either drawing: Br, Cl, \(CH_{3}\) and Me. 'Me' IS a methyl group, so the carbon carries TWO identical methyl groups and only three distinct substituents. It therefore is not a stereocentre at all, and the compound is simply 2-bromo-2-chloropropane, which is achiral.

The two pictures differ only by exchanging the wedge \(Cl\) and the dashed \(CH_{3}\) from left to right, i.e. they are mirror images through a vertical plane. Because the molecule is achiral it is superimposable on its mirror image, so the two structures represent the SAME compound.

They cannot be enantiomers or diastereomers (no stereocentre exists), and 'meso' is meaningless here since that term needs at least two stereocentres. Hence they are identical molecules.

The five compounds read from the figures are (A) phenol, (B) 4-nitrophenol, (C) 4-methoxyphenol, (D) 4-nitrobenzoic acid and (E) benzoic acid.

First split them by class. Carboxylic acids are far stronger acids than phenols, because the carboxylate anion delocalises the charge over two equivalent electronegative oxygens, whereas the phenoxide charge is spread over carbon atoms of the ring. So (D) and (E) both outrank (A), (B) and (C).

Within the acids: the \(p\)-nitro group is strongly electron withdrawing by both \(-I\) and \(-R\), stabilising the carboxylate, so \((D) > (E)\) (\(pK_{a}\) about \(3.4\) against \(4.2\)).

Within the phenols: \(p\)-nitro again stabilises the phenoxide strongly, so (B) is the most acidic phenol (\(pK_{a}\) about \(7.1\)). The \(p\)-methoxy group is electron releasing by resonance, which destabilises the phenoxide, so (C) is weaker than plain phenol (\(pK_{a}\) about \(10.2\) against \(10.0\)).

Descending acidity: \((D) > (E) > (B) > (A) > (C)\).
authoredSolutions.42:
The four compounds are (A) aniline, (B) 4-methoxyaniline, (C) 4-nitroaniline and (D) 4-methylaniline.

The strongest conjugate acid is produced by the WEAKEST base, because a weak base holds the proton loosely and its protonated form gives it up readily.

Ranking the bases: the \(p\)-nitro group withdraws electron density powerfully by \(-I\) and \(-R\), pulling the nitrogen lone pair further into the ring and making 4-nitroaniline by far the weakest base of the set. The \(p\)-methoxy and \(p\)-methyl groups are electron releasing, so those two anilines are stronger bases than aniline itself.

Since 4-nitroaniline is the weakest base, its anilinium ion is the strongest conjugate acid. Answer (C).

An aldotetrose has the skeleton \(CHO-CHOH-CHOH-CH_{2}OH\), with two stereocentres, and concentrated \(HNO_{3}\) oxidises BOTH terminal groups (\(CHO\) and \(CH_{2}OH\)) to \(COOH\), giving a tartaric acid.

The product will be OPTICALLY INACTIVE only if it is meso-tartaric acid, which requires the two hydroxyl groups to lie on the SAME side of the Fischer projection; that internal mirror plane then cancels the rotation. If the hydroxyls are on opposite sides the product is an optically active tartaric acid.

The two hydroxyls on the same side means the sugar is erythrose, not threose. The 'D' prefix is fixed by the lowest stereocentre (C-3), whose \(OH\) must point to the RIGHT.

So we need the Fischer projection with the C-2 \(OH\) on the right AND the C-3 \(OH\) on the right, which is D-erythrose. Among the four printed structures only option (C) has both hydroxyl groups on the right-hand side. Option (A) has both on the left (L-erythrose, also giving meso acid but wrong series), and options (B) and (D) have them on opposite sides (threoses, giving optically active tartaric acid).

Sort the four cations by their qualitative-analysis group. \(Pb^{2+}\) and \(Cu^{2+}\) belong to group II and are precipitated as sulphides by \(H_{2}S\) in DILUTE HCl. \(Fe^{3+}\) belongs to group III and is precipitated as \(Fe(OH)_{3}\) by \(NH_{4}OH\) in the presence of \(NH_{4}Cl\), before any \(H_{2}S\) is passed. \(Mn^{2+}\) belongs to group IV, whose group reagent is exactly \(H_{2}S\) in the presence of \(NH_{4}OH\): the ammoniacal medium raises \([S^{2-}]\) enough to exceed the solubility product of the more soluble MnS, which precipitates as buff-coloured manganese(II) sulphide.

So the cation described is \(Mn^{2+}\). Manganese has the configuration \([Ar]3d^{5}4s^{2}\), so all seven of these electrons can be involved in bonding and its highest possible oxidation state is \(+7\), realised in \(MnO_{4}^{-}\) and \(Mn_{2}O_{7}\).

Matching each with its characteristic test: a secondary alcohol such as cyclohexanol is distinguished by the Victor Meyer test; a primary amine such as cyclohexylamine responds to Hinsberg's reagent test, which classifies amines by the solubility of the sulphonamide formed; an aldehyde such as cyclohexanecarbaldehyde gives a positive Tollens' silver-mirror test; and phenol couples with a diazonium salt to give a coloured azo compound, the dye test.

A bomb calorimeter works at constant VOLUME, so the measured heat is \(\Delta U\), not \(\Delta H\).

Moles of ethanol: \(M(C_{2}H_{5}OH) = 46\ g\ mol^{-1}\), so \(n = 3.365/46 = 0.07315\ mol\).
\(\Delta U_{comb} = -99.472/0.07315 = -1359.8\ kJ\ mol^{-1}\).

Combustion equation: \(C_{2}H_{5}OH(l) + 3O_{2}(g) \rightarrow 2CO_{2}(g) + 3H_{2}O(l)\), so \(\Delta n_{g} = 2 - 3 = -1\).
\(\Delta H = \Delta U + \Delta n_{g}RT = -1359.8 + (-1)(8.314 \times 10^{-3})(298.15) = -1359.8 - 2.48 = -1362.3\ kJ\ mol^{-1}\).

Apply Hess's law to the same equation:
\(\Delta H_{comb} = 2\Delta H_{f}(CO_{2}) + 3\Delta H_{f}(H_{2}O) - \Delta H_{f}(C_{2}H_{5}OH)\)
\(-1362.3 = 2(-393.5) + 3(-285.8) - \Delta H_{f}\)
\(-1362.3 = -787.0 - 857.4 - \Delta H_{f} = -1644.4 - \Delta H_{f}\)
\(\Delta H_{f} = -1644.4 + 1362.3 = -282.1\ kJ\ mol^{-1}\)

Hence \(|\Delta H_{f}^{\circ}| = 282\ kJ\ mol^{-1}\) (nearest integer).

Take 2 mol of \(N_{2}O_{5}\) as the basis for \(2N_{2}O_{5}(g) \rightleftharpoons 2N_{2}O_{4}(g) + O_{2}(g)\).

With 50 percent dissociation, 1 mol of \(N_{2}O_{5}\) reacts, producing 1 mol \(N_{2}O_{4}\) and \(0.5\) mol \(O_{2}\):
at equilibrium \(N_{2}O_{5} = 1\), \(N_{2}O_{4} = 1\), \(O_{2} = 0.5\), total \(= 2.5\ mol\).

Mole fractions are \(0.4, 0.4, 0.2\); with \(P_{total} = 2\ atm\) the partial pressures are \(0.8, 0.8, 0.4\ atm\).

\(K_{p} = \frac{(p_{N_{2}O_{4}})^{2}(p_{O_{2}})}{(p_{N_{2}O_{5}})^{2}} = \frac{(0.8)^{2}(0.4)}{(0.8)^{2}} = 0.4\)

At \(T = 50 + 273 = 323\ K\):
\(\Delta G^{\circ} = -2.303RT\log K_{p}\)
\(\log 0.4 = 2\log 2 - 1 = 0.60 - 1 = -0.40\)
\(\Delta G^{\circ} = -2.303(8.314)(323)(-0.40) = +2473.8\ J\ mol^{-1}\)

The magnitude is \(x = 2474\ J\ mol^{-1}\). The positive sign is expected, since \(K_{p} < 1\) means the reaction is not spontaneous under standard conditions.

The couple with the higher reduction potential is the cathode, so \(M^{x+}/M\) (\(+0.15\ V\)) is reduced and Fe is oxidised.
\(E^{\circ}_{cell} = E^{\circ}_{cathode} - E^{\circ}_{anode} = 0.15 - (-0.036) = 0.186\ V\)

Balance the cell reaction. Cathode: \(M^{x+} + xe^{-} \rightarrow M\); anode: \(Fe \rightarrow Fe^{3+} + 3e^{-}\). Combining gives \(3M^{x+} + xFe \rightarrow 3M + xFe^{3+}\), so \(n = 3x\) electrons are transferred.

Nernst equation:
\(E_{cell} = E^{\circ}_{cell} - \frac{0.059}{n}\log Q\)
\(0.2057 = 0.186 - \frac{0.059}{n}\log(10^{-2}) = 0.186 + \frac{0.059 \times 2}{n}\)
\(0.2057 - 0.186 = 0.0197 = \frac{0.118}{n}\)
\(n = \frac{0.118}{0.0197} \approx 6\)

Since \(n = 3x\), \(x = 2\). This is consistent with the hint that M is a p-block metal, the \(+2\) state being the inert-pair-stabilised state of tin or lead.

For a first order reaction \(k = \frac{2.303}{t}\log\frac{[A]_{0}}{[A]}\), so the time taken depends only on the RATIO by which the concentration falls.

From \(t = 0\) to \(t = 20\ min\) the concentration goes \(0.6500 \rightarrow 0.00065\), a fall by a factor of \(1000\):
\(k = \frac{2.303}{20}\log 1000 = \frac{2.303 \times 3}{20} = 0.3455\ min^{-1}\)

From \(t = 0\) to \(t = x\) the concentration goes \(0.6500 \rightarrow 0.0650\), a fall by a factor of \(10\):
\(x = \frac{2.303}{k}\log 10 = \frac{2.303}{0.3455} = 6.67\ min\)

Equivalently, one factor of ten is one third of three factors of ten, so \(x = 20/3 = 6.67\ min\), which to the nearest integer is \(7\ min\).
